title: Post Quantum Sphinx
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage has no layered packet format; this is the packet-format building block for hiding sender and path in a successor, and shows the size cost of post-quantum per-hop keys.
note: Two Sphinx variants: NIKE Sphinx with a hybrid NIKE (X25519 + CTIDH512, isogeny assumption) that keeps the compact blinded group-element header, and KEM Sphinx that replaces the group element by one KEM ciphertext per hop inside the routing-info block, so the header grows linearly with hop count but each hop does one public-key operation instead of two (about 2x faster server side). Hybrid KEM must use a security-preserving combiner (IND-CCA2). No byte table in the paper; with X-Wing (1120 B ciphertext) a 5-hop KEM header carries about 5.6 KB of ciphertexts (derived).

title: Outfox: a Postquantum Packet Format for Layered Mixnets
bitmessage_link: Quantifies how per-hop post-quantum KEMs multiply packet size, the cost any flooded or mixed successor pays on every message.
note: Sphinx replacement for fixed-length layered routes with one KEM ciphertext per layer (UC security proof). Table 6 sizes (bytes) public key/ciphertext: X25519 32/32, ML-KEM-768 1184/1088, X-Wing 1216/1120, Classic McEliece mceliece460896f 524160/188. Packet at layer 0 = 10k+|m|+2(l+1)p+4lk bits for l+1 layers and ciphertext length p, so 4 layers with X-Wing add about 9 KB of KEM ciphertexts. Measured on Ryzen 5 3600: KEM.Enc 69.6 us (X25519) vs 14.5 us (ML-KEM-768), 84.3 us (X-Wing), 50.3 ms (McEliece). Assumptions: IND-CCA KEM, AEAD, committing.

title: Echomix: a Strong Anonymity System with Messaging
bitmessage_link: A deployed-design answer to Bitmessage's weaknesses (recipient ambiguity by flooding, no source anonymity) that already carries post-quantum hybrid keys.
note: Katzenpost design: post-quantum hybrid Sphinx (NIKE and KEM variants), decoy traffic, mixing strategy and a messaging layer; threat model includes a global passive adversary, compromised contacts and quantum decryption. Byte sizes are given by the KEM Sphinx specification rather than here.

title: Mixnet Research Review
bitmessage_link: Survey context for what replaces Bitmessage's flood-and-trial-decrypt design.
note: Literature overview of mix network designs, packet formats and attacks written by the Katzenpost team; used to place post-quantum Sphinx, Outfox and decoy/stratified designs.

title: Provable Security for the Onion Routing and Mix Network Packet Format Sphinx
bitmessage_link: Security baseline for the packet format most successor designs reuse.
note: Shows DDH is not enough for the original Sphinx proof and that the Gap Diffie-Hellman assumption is needed; proves a slightly adapted Sphinx secure under GDH. Relevant to post-quantum ports because the blinded-group-element trick needs a NIKE (CSIDH/CTIDH or lattice NIKEs are not drop-in), which is why KEM-based formats (KEM Sphinx, Outfox) were proposed.

title: Onion Routing with Replies
note: First UC framework and two instantiations for onion routing with protected replies (updatable encryption; SNARG-authenticated payloads). Classical assumptions; the SNARG route and per-hop re-encryption bring large proofs/ciphertexts that a post-quantum port would have to replace with lattice or hash-based equivalents.
bitmessage_link: Gives anonymous reply paths, which Bitmessage lacks (a reply reveals the sender address).

title: Post-Quantum Forward-Secure Onion Routing (Future Anonymity in Today's Budget)
note: HybridOR: hybrid one-way authenticated key exchange secure under ring-LWE or gap-DH, drop-in for ntor with existing DH node keys. Client sends 1312 B (a ring element of about 1280 B plus a 32 B curve point); node reply about 1.4 KB (derived from 1/8(n lg q + n) + 32 for n=512, q=1051649). Compare 139625 B and 10075 B for earlier lattice AKEs they reject. Motivation: record-now-decrypt-later against Tor traffic.
bitmessage_link: Early evidence that anonymity networks need post-quantum forward secrecy because recorded traffic is the threat; same record-everything adversary Bitmessage faces.

title: A quantum-safe circuit-extension handshake for Tor
venue: NIST Workshop on Cybersecurity in a Post-Quantum World, 2015
note: Adds NTRUEncrypt key exchange in parallel with ntor (hybrid, minimal change); most extra cost falls on the client. Tor CREATE handshake data is capped near 505 bytes, so a lattice key does not fit without widening cells. Basis for Tor proposals 263 and 269 and the PoPETs 2016 paper by the same authors.
bitmessage_link: Concrete example of a fixed small cell (Tor 512 B) colliding with post-quantum key sizes, the same pressure a size-limited flooded object feels.

title: Tor proposal 263: Request to change key exchange protocol for handshake v1.2
note: Proposes NTRU (EES443EP2) key exchange alongside ntor for circuit extension; encrypted message limited to m <= 49 bytes; depends on proposal 249 (CREATE cells with more than 505 bytes of handshake data) because the lattice material exceeds one cell. Superseded by proposal 269.
bitmessage_link: Documents the cell-size obstacle to post-quantum handshakes in a deployed anonymity network.

title: Tor proposal 269: Transitionally secure hybrid handshakes
note: Generic hybrid ntor replacement: client sends ID, KEYID, DH share X and KEM public key EPK; server returns Y, KEM ciphertext C and an authentication tag, with the shared secret a KDF of both. Parameter-generic (KEM_PK_LEN, KEM_C_LEN), so ML-KEM-768 (1184 B key, 1088 B ciphertext) or sntrup761 (1158 B key, 1039 B ciphertext, as commonly cited) fit once cells are widened or fragmented (see 340).
bitmessage_link: The reference design for retrofitting a post-quantum KEM into an anonymity network handshake.

title: Tor proposal 340: Packed and fragmented relay messages
note: Lets relay messages exceed one cell by packing and fragmentation; relay cell body 509 - 16 = 493 bytes (498 before), cell authentication digest grows from 4 to 14 bytes. Needed so post-quantum handshake messages (ML-KEM-768 key 1184 B) can cross circuits.
bitmessage_link: Shows the engineering price of larger post-quantum objects in a fixed-cell network.

title: Post Quantum Migration of Tor
note: Inventories Tor's primitives and estimates the cost of replacing them. Key sizes in bytes: ML-KEM encapsulation key/decapsulation key/ciphertext as in FIPS 203, HQC-128/192/256 encapsulation key 2249/4522/7245; ML-DSA key plus signature 3732 B; Tor CREATE handshake limit 505 B versus 693 B for ntruees443ep1; only ML-KEM-512/768 and sntrup761 (KEMs) and Falcon-512 and ML-DSA-44 (signatures) are judged viable. Estimated added circuit latency about 83 ms (theoretical, from liboqs benchmarks).
bitmessage_link: Best single costing of post-quantum primitives inside an anonymity network; sizes translate to per-message cost in a flooding successor.

title: QSOR: Quantum-Safe Onion Routing
note: Benchmarks six NIST level-1 KEMs in a SweetOnions Tor simulation. FrodoKEM-640 ciphertext is 9720 B (many cells); SIKE (broken in 2022) was the only candidate whose ciphertext fits one 512 B Tor cell. Proposes a pure and a hybrid quantum-safe circuit creation. Result predates ML-KEM standardization.
bitmessage_link: Early size and latency data for post-quantum KEMs in onion circuits.

title: Aquaman: A Transparent Proxy Architecture for Quantum Resilient Key Establishment
note: Harvest-now-decrypt-later framing; proxy offloads PQC or splits a session key across diverse media with recovery probability decaying as (B/d)^n; 1000-run EC2 prototype. Weak relevance: engineering prototype, no anonymity analysis.
bitmessage_link: Illustrates the record-now-decrypt-later threat model; limited technical overlap.

title: Onion-Routed Multi-Circuit Key Establishment for Quantum-Resilient Sessions
note: Splits a session key into fragments sent over distinct ephemeral Tor circuits so an adversary must deanonymize every circuit; prototype takes 13-20 s on average (about 88% Tor delay). Argument is a correlation bound, not a post-quantum primitive.
bitmessage_link: Alternative to post-quantum primitives for long-term confidentiality; relies on the anonymity network itself.

title: Post-Quantum Anonymous One-Sided Authenticated Key Exchange without Random Oracles
note: Generic constructions of anonymous one-sided AKE (client anonymous, server authenticated, as in Tor and Riffle) in the ROM and standard model; first post-quantum instantiation is isogeny-based (SIDH-era, since broken), so only the generic KEM-style framework carries over to ML-KEM.
bitmessage_link: Formal model for the key exchange an anonymous client runs with each relay or mailbox.

title: How to Hide MetaData in MLS-Like Secure Group Messaging: Simple, Modular, and Post-Quantum
bitmessage_link: Shows how recipient anonymity and group membership can be hidden without flooding while remaining post-quantum, relevant to Bitmessage chans.
note: Modular transform hiding sender and group-membership metadata in MLS-style continuous group key agreement from key-private PKE and hybrid encryption; the building blocks are instantiated post-quantum (lattice KEMs with anonymity). Overhead is quantified relative to plain MLS; ciphertext sizes follow the underlying KEM (ML-KEM-768: 1088 B).

title: Bundled Authenticated Key Exchange: A Concrete Treatment of (Post-Quantum) Signal's Handshake Protocol
note: Unified model for prekey-bundle handshakes; shows X3DH and PQXDH (harvest-now-decrypt-later secure, not fully post-quantum authenticated) fall short of optimal security and proposes RingXKEM, a fully post-quantum handshake sharing state across prekey bundles, with a size and efficiency comparison.
bitmessage_link: Static-key encryption is Bitmessage's weakness; this is the formal treatment of the asynchronous handshake that fixes it, post-quantum.

title: Two Practical and Provably Secure Block Ciphers: BEAR and LION
note: Wide-block ciphers (hash plus stream cipher, 3 or 4 Feistel rounds) from which LIONESS, the SPRP used for Sphinx payloads, derives. Symmetric only: Grover halves key strength, so 256-bit keys keep 128-bit post-quantum security; the post-quantum cost in Sphinx comes entirely from the public-key header.
bitmessage_link: Payload cipher family behind Sphinx-style formats; unaffected by size growth of KEMs.

title: Oblivious Message Retrieval
bitmessage_link: Direct replacement for Bitmessage's download-everything-and-trial-decrypt, with a large key and server-compute price.
note: Outsources trial decryption to an untrusted server using homomorphic encryption (BFV, ring-LWE, so plausibly post-quantum) so the server never learns which messages are for whom. Costs: clue under 1 kB after optimization; one-time detection (public) key of about 129 MB for OMRp2 (about 16 MB for OMRp1); detection time practical but per-recipient server work linear in the board.

title: Group Oblivious Message Retrieval
note: OMR for multi-recipient messages; builds the first lattice-based key-private multi-recipient encryption (KP-MRE). Reported parameters (D,Q,t)=(2^15,~2850,65537) with 612-byte payload. Assumptions: ring/module LWE.
bitmessage_link: Addresses chans/group delivery without flooding; recipient set hidden by key-private encryption.

title: PerfOMR: Oblivious Message Retrieval with Reduced Communication and Computation
bitmessage_link: Current efficiency frontier for hiding the recipient without a flood, with sizes a flooded object could carry.
note: Ring-LWE based OMR; about 1 kB overhead per message (clue), public (clue) key about 132 kB, detection under a second per 1 million messages-class workloads versus >100 kB ciphertexts in earlier constructions; plausibly post-quantum. Spam-DoS resistance is incomplete (see Snake-eye).

title: Snake-eye Resistant PKE from LWE for Oblivious Message Retrieval and Robust Encryption
note: Proves OMRp2 DoS-resistant under LWE, shows PerfOMR-style schemes are attackable by malicious senders, and builds LWEmongrass (snake-eye resistant PKE, hence robust PKE); DoS-PerfOMR is 12x faster than OMRp2.
bitmessage_link: Spam by malicious senders is Bitmessage's reason for proof-of-work; here it is a cryptographic property.

title: One Server for the Price of Two: Simple and Fast Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
bitmessage_link: PIR is the other route to hiding which object a client fetches; shows the hint-size cost.
note: LWE-based single-server PIR at near memory bandwidth. For a 1 GB database SimplePIR needs a 121 MB client hint and 242 KB per query; DoublePIR shrinks the hint to 16 MB at 345 KB per query with slightly lower throughput. Security: plain LWE, post-quantum.

title: FrodoPIR: Simple, Scalable, Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
note: LWE-only PIR with an offline phase done by the server alone; under 1 s per query and small response blow-up on a 1 million x 1 KB database; avoids FHE machinery. Security: plain LWE (post-quantum).
bitmessage_link: Practical lattice PIR for mailbox-style retrieval instead of broadcast.

title: YPIR: High-Throughput Single-Server PIR with Silent Preprocessing
bitmessage_link: Shows PIR can run without per-client state, a requirement for ephemeral anonymous clients.
note: Removes the offline hint of SimplePIR-family schemes: 2.5 MB total communication with no hint, throughput up to 83% of memory bandwidth, and 10-15x lower server preprocessing; a variant with a 724 MB hint reaches 1.5 MB communication. Post-quantum (LWE/RLWE).

title: Spiral: Fast, High-Rate Single-Server PIR via FHE Composition
bitmessage_link: Reference point for query/response expansion in lattice PIR.
note: Composes Regev and GSW ciphertexts (ring-LWE) for high-rate PIR; reported query sizes of tens of KB and response rate near 0.5 for large records. Post-quantum assumptions.

title: Hintless Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
note: PIR with no client-side hint (and no offline preprocessing) from LWE with a modest communication increase compared with SimplePIR-style schemes; post-quantum.
bitmessage_link: Stateless lattice PIR suitable for a client that cannot keep per-server state.

title: Post-Quantum Privacy Pass via Post-Quantum Anonymous Credentials
note: Anonymous credential from zkDilithium (a STARK-friendly Dilithium2 variant) plus zkSTARK proofs; token size trades 85-175 KB against generation time, verification 20-30 ms, verifier RAM under 5 MB; comparable to best post-quantum blind signatures (22-100 KB). Supports rate-limited Privacy Pass. Assumptions: module-LWE/SIS plus hash-based STARKs.
bitmessage_link: Anonymous rate limiting is the post-quantum alternative to Bitmessage proof-of-work; the token size shows why it is hard to attach to every flooded object.

title: Lattice Signature with Efficient Protocols, Application to Anonymous Credentials
note: First lattice anonymous credential with practical sizes: proof of message-signature possession under 650 KB; showing a credential with 10 attributes of 128 bits and 4 disclosed below 730 KB. Earlier approaches needed tens to hundreds of MB. Assumptions: MSIS/MLWE-type.
bitmessage_link: Upper bound on what a post-quantum anonymous admission proof costs per message.

title: Lattice-based Commit-Transferrable Signatures and Applications to Anonymous Credentials
note: Commit-transferrable signature primitive plus lattice NIZKPoK gives a modular anonymous credential with smaller proofs than earlier lattice constructions; post-quantum under SIS/LWE.
bitmessage_link: Candidate admission credential in place of per-object proof-of-work.

title: Everlasting Anonymous Rate-Limited Tokens
note: Anonymous rate-limited tokens whose anonymity survives later quantum attack on stored tokens (everlasting privacy) while unforgeability may rely on classical assumptions; dispenser yields up to k unlinkable tokens. Explicit answer to record-now-decrypt-later for token metadata.
bitmessage_link: Separates long-term privacy from short-term unforgeability: exactly the asymmetry an admission check on a flooded network needs.

title: Lattice-Based Blind Signatures: Short, Efficient, and Round-Optimal
note: Two-round blind signature, signature 22 KB, transcript as small as 60 KB; standard lattice assumptions (Ring/Module-SIS, LWE, NTRU). Compare roughly 45 KB for Agrawal et al. and about 100 KB for del Pino-Katsumata.
bitmessage_link: Sets the floor for post-quantum anonymous token size, orders of magnitude above a 64-byte ECDSA signature.

title: Practical, Round-Optimal Lattice-Based Blind Signatures
note: First practical round-optimal lattice blind signature with unbounded signing queries: signature slightly above 45 KB at 109-bit core-SVP security; rests on a new one-more-ISIS assumption.
bitmessage_link: Baseline size for post-quantum blind issuance of admission tokens.

title: Practical Post-Quantum Signatures for Privacy
note: Lattice signature with efficient protocols, aimed at privacy-preserving constructions such as anonymous credentials and group-style signatures, with concrete parameters smaller than earlier lattice proofs of possession.
bitmessage_link: Candidate group-signature or credential primitive for per-sender rate limiting.

title: Lattice-Based Group Signatures: Achieving Full Dynamicity (and Deniability) with Ease
note: Fully dynamic lattice group signature (join and revoke) with a simple design; sizes are in the hundreds of KB per signature (impractical to attach per message).
bitmessage_link: Group signature route to anonymous-but-accountable posting, post-quantum.

title: Privacy-Preserving Authentication: Theory vs. Practice
note: Survey of anonymous credentials, group/ring signatures and deployed systems, including the state of post-quantum constructions and why none is yet competitive with classical sizes.
bitmessage_link: Orientation on rate-limiting and anonymous-admission primitives.

title: Post Quantum Fuzzy Stealth Signatures and Applications
note: Post-quantum stealth signatures with fuzzy matching (a tunable false-positive rate reduces the recipient's scanning set), built from lattices; applications include private payments and retrieval.
bitmessage_link: Fuzzy detection is a middle path between trial-decrypting everything and full OMR.

title: Post-Quantum Stealth Address Protocols
note: Three lattice stealth address protocols (LWE, Ring-LWE, Module-LWE); Module-LWE (Kyber-style) SAP scans the ephemeral public key registry about 66.8% faster than the elliptic-curve pairing SAP. Recipient detection is scan-and-test, so ciphertext size sets scanning bandwidth.
bitmessage_link: Stealth addressing has the same recipient-scan cost structure as Bitmessage's trial decryption; post-quantum version quantifies it.

title: Key-Privacy in Public-Key Encryption
note: Defines key-privacy (IK-CPA/IK-CCA, i.e. ANO-CPA/ANO-CCA): a ciphertext must not reveal the recipient key. Every post-quantum KEM used for recipient-hiding must be re-proved against this notion.
bitmessage_link: The property Bitmessage's flooding relies on: ciphertext must not reveal which key it targets.

title: Anonymous, Robust Post-Quantum Public Key Encryption
note: Shows Fujisaki-Okamoto-derived PKE can be ANO-CCA anonymous and robust (no false decryptions to the wrong key) in the ROM/QROM, and flags that Kyber/Saber/NTRU-type KEMs lacked such proofs. Robustness matters for trial decryption: a wrong key must not accept a ciphertext.
bitmessage_link: Anonymity and robustness are exactly what trial decryption needs; this transfers them to post-quantum schemes.

title: Anonymity of NIST PQC Round 3 KEMs
note: Analyses ANO-CCA of all Round-3 KEMs: NTRU, BIKE, FrodoKEM, NTRU LPRime and SIKE are anonymous in the QROM; Classic McEliece needs a strongly disjoint-simulatable PKE; HQC fails for two of three parameter sets in the then-current design; Kyber and Saber had a gap in the QROM IND-CCA proof. Supersedes ePrint 2021/741.
bitmessage_link: First systematic answer to whether post-quantum KEM ciphertexts hide the recipient key.

title: Post-Quantum Anonymity of Kyber
note: Proves Kyber and hybrid PKE built from it are ANO-CCA secure in the QROM under MLWE (the 'hidden' ciphertext includes an FO re-encryption check). Result applies to the Kyber round-3 design; ML-KEM (FIPS 203) differs slightly in hashing the public key and implicit rejection, so a one-line re-check is needed.
bitmessage_link: Justifies using Kyber/ML-KEM ciphertexts as recipient-anonymous objects in a flooded network.

title: Revisiting Anonymity in Post-quantum Public Key Encryption
note: Proves ANO-CCA for FO-derived KEMs with implicit rejection (including textbook FO without the extra hash) in the QROM and for KEM-DEM hybrid encryption, explicit and implicit rejection. No open copy located.
bitmessage_link: Tightens the anonymity proofs needed for recipient-hiding hybrid encryption.

title: Keeping Up with the KEMs: Stronger Security Notions for KEMs and Automated Analysis of KEM-based Protocols
bitmessage_link: Anonymity needs binding-style properties on top of IND-CCA when one ciphertext is tried against many keys.
note: Generalises and strengthens KEM security notions, adding binding properties (the shared secret binds the public key and ciphertext, in honest, leaky and malicious variants) and a Tamarin library for KEM-based protocols; finds re-encapsulation attacks that IND-CCA misses. Reports follow-up attacks (Schmieg) on ML-KEM MAL-BIND-K-PK and MAL-BIND-K-CT, caused by decapsulation relying on the stored hash of the key. Needed when one ciphertext is tried against many keys.

title: Hybrid Obfuscated Key Exchange and KEMs
note: First OKEM combiner with hybrid IND-CCA security and hybrid ciphertext-obfuscation guarantees (public keys and ciphertexts that look like random bitstrings), used to build Drivel, a pq-obfs variant for hybrid obfs4. Plain hybrid KEM combiners do not give hybrid obfuscation. Builds on Kemeleon, which encodes ML-KEM keys and ciphertexts as random-looking strings under decision module-LWE (not statistically indistinguishable).
bitmessage_link: Random-looking post-quantum ciphertexts are the precondition for recipient-anonymous flooding and for censorship-resistant transport.

title: Obfuscated Key Exchange
note: Formalizes obfuscated key exchange and obfuscated KEMs (OKEMs) and proposes pq-obfs, a post-quantum drop-in for Tor's obfs4 using ML-KEM encodings.
bitmessage_link: Handshake indistinguishability for transport under a global observer; pairs with ciphertext key-privacy.

title: Anonymity of X-Wing and its Variants
note: First anonymity analysis of X-Wing (ML-KEM-768 + X25519; 1216 B public key, 1120 B ciphertext). Proves in the standard model that weak anonymity of any IND-CCA KEM implies full ANO-CCA (tight, memory-tight), then in the ROM that X-Wing is weakly anonymous if both X25519 (unconditionally) and ML-KEM-768 are; proposes a memory-tight variant and improves the original IND-CCA proof.
bitmessage_link: First anonymity proof for the default hybrid KEM, so hybrid post-quantum ciphertexts can serve as recipient-hidden objects.

title: X-Wing: The Hybrid KEM You've Been Looking For
bitmessage_link: Default sizes for a hybrid per-message or per-hop encapsulation (about 1.1 KB of ciphertext overhead).
note: Concrete hybrid KEM: ML-KEM-768 plus X25519 combined by SHA3-256 over the shared secrets, X25519 ciphertext and public key (and a fixed label), dropping the ML-KEM ciphertext. Sizes: public key 1216 B, ciphertext 1120 B, shared secret 32 B, 32-byte decapsulation seed. IND-CCA if the strong-DH assumption holds in the X25519 group, or if ML-KEM-768 is IND-CCA and SHA3-256 is a PRF.

title: X-Wing: general-purpose hybrid post-quantum KEM (Internet-Draft)
note: Specification of X-Wing: 32-byte secret key seed, 1216-byte encapsulation key (1184 ML-KEM + 32 X25519), 1120-byte ciphertext (1088 + 32), 32-byte shared secret; KEM combiner SHA3-256(ss_M || ss_X || ct_X || pk_X || label).
bitmessage_link: Implementable spec for the hybrid KEM that Outfox and Katzenpost instantiate.

title: Hybrid Key Encapsulation Mechanisms and Authenticated Key Exchange
note: Formalises hybrid KEMs (IND-CPA/CCA preservation by concatenating or XOR-ing component outputs, with caveats) and hybrid authenticated key exchange; the hybrid ciphertext is the concatenation of component ciphertexts, so sizes add.
bitmessage_link: Theory behind the hybrid wrappers used in post-quantum onion and mix formats.

title: KEM Combiners
bitmessage_link: Combiner correctness is what makes hybrid per-hop KEMs safe.
note: Defines generic KEM combiners that stay IND-CCA if at least one input KEM is; the standard-model constructions hash shared keys together with all ciphertexts, which is why naive combiners carry every ciphertext (X-Wing removes the ML-KEM ciphertext by specialisation).

title: The Best of Both KEMs: Securely Combining KEMs in Post-quantum Hybrid Schemes
note: Generalises X-Wing: when combining several KEMs, one may omit the ciphertext of any KEM with ciphertext second-preimage resistance (C2PRI) provided the key combiner is a split-key PRF. Saves up to a full component ciphertext (1088 B for ML-KEM-768) per hybrid encapsulation.
bitmessage_link: Directly reduces the per-hop or per-message size cost of hybrid post-quantum encryption.

title: Kopis: A KEM for Obfuscation
note: Module-LWE based KEM specified so that public keys and ciphertexts are uniform bytestrings, removing the hash-to-vector, matrix-expansion and ciphertext-decompression machinery that obfuscating protocols (PAKE, OKEX) need to bolt onto ML-KEM. Alternative to Kemeleon encodings.
bitmessage_link: Candidate recipient-anonymous, random-looking encapsulation for hidden-recipient objects.

title: Security Analysis of Signal's PQXDH Handshake
bitmessage_link: Static prekeys with a post-quantum KEM are the closest deployed analogue to fixing Bitmessage's static-key encryption.
note: Game-based 'maximum-exposure' analysis of PQXDH (X3DH plus a post-quantum KEM; Signal uses Kyber-1024) with concrete classical and post-quantum session-key security bounds. Shows the design needs a KEM binding property (re-encapsulation attacks otherwise), that Kyber and ML-KEM satisfy the novel binding notion they define, and that missing domain separation lowers achievable security. Authentication stays classical, but signing of prekeys adds a post-quantum flavour.

title: Triple Ratchet: A Bandwidth Efficient Hybrid-Secure Signal Protocol
bitmessage_link: Shows how to amortise post-quantum key sizes across a message stream, the opposite of paying them on every flooded object.
note: Hybrid-secure Signal ratchet whose PQ-ratchet uses erasure codes so communication is balanced even in bad delivery patterns, plus Katana, a Kyber variant cutting the combined public key plus ciphertext from 2272 B (1184 + 1088, ML-KEM-768, 71x a 32 B X25519 share) to 1416 B at 192-bit security (hint-MLWE assumption); notes PQ3 pays the PQ ratchet only about every 50 messages to amortise Kyber cost. Basis of Signal SPQR.

title: A Formal Analysis of Apple's iMessage PQ3 Protocol
note: Tamarin analysis of Apple PQ3: ECDH ratcheting plus periodic ML-KEM rekeying (ML-KEM-768 for ephemeral KEM keys, ML-KEM-1024 for prekeys, 1568 B key and ciphertext). Establishes forward secrecy and post-compromise security including post-quantum, with caveats on authentication.
bitmessage_link: Second deployed example of amortising post-quantum key material in a messenger.

title: The PQXDH Key Agreement Protocol
bitmessage_link: Specification of a deployed asynchronous post-quantum handshake.
note: Adds a Kyber-1024 KEM prekey (1568-byte public key, 1568-byte ciphertext) to X3DH; the initial message carries one ciphertext; authentication and deniability stay classical (EdDSA/XEdDSA). Provides post-quantum forward secrecy against harvest-now-decrypt-later only.

title: FIPS 203: Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard (ML-KEM)
bitmessage_link: Sets the minimum per-recipient or per-hop size growth (about 34x over X25519) for any successor using the standard KEM.
note: Sizes in bytes (encapsulation key / decapsulation key / ciphertext / shared secret): ML-KEM-512 800/1632/768/32, ML-KEM-768 1184/2400/1088/32, ML-KEM-1024 1568/3168/1568/32. Security: module-LWE with FO transform and implicit rejection; categories 1/3/5. The 1088-byte ciphertext replaces a 32-byte X25519 share.

title: FIPS 204: Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA)
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage signs every object with ECDSA (about 70 B); this is the post-quantum cost of keeping that.
note: Sizes in bytes (public key / private key / signature): ML-DSA-44 1312/2560/2420, ML-DSA-65 1952/4032/3309, ML-DSA-87 2592/4896/4627. Module-LWE and module-SIS (Fiat-Shamir with aborts). Compare Ed25519 32/64/64: a signed flooded object grows by 2.4-4.6 KB, and key distribution by 1.3-2.6 KB.

title: FIPS 205: Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard (SLH-DSA)
bitmessage_link: Most conservative post-quantum signature; sizes show why per-message signatures cannot be hash-based.
note: Hash-only security assumptions. Public key 32/48/64 B, signature bytes: SLH-DSA-128s 7856, 128f 17088, 192s 16224, 192f 35664, 256s 29792, 256f 49856. Small variants (s) sign slowly; fast variants (f) are 2x larger. Per-object signatures of 8-50 KB are infeasible for flooded message objects.

title: NIST IR 8545: Status Report on the Fourth Round of the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization Process
note: Selects HQC (code-based, quasi-cyclic syndrome decoding) as a backup KEM to ML-KEM, with a draft standard planned; BIKE and Classic McEliece not selected. Table 7 (bytes) for HQC-128/192/256: encapsulation key 2249/4522/7245, decapsulation key 40, ciphertext 4497/9042/14485; BIKE level 1/3/5 for comparison: key 1541/3083/5122, ciphertext 1573/3115/5154. The 2025 HQC specification later changes these to 2241/4514/7237 and 4433/8978/14421. HQC ciphertexts are 4-9x those of ML-KEM.
bitmessage_link: HQC's multi-KB ciphertexts make it unusable per message in a flooding network; relevant only as an algorithm-diversity backup.

title: Hamming Quasi-Cyclic (HQC): specification, 22 August 2025
note: Sizes in bytes (encapsulation key / decapsulation key / ciphertext / shared key): HQC-1 2241/2321/4433/32, HQC-3 4514/4602/8978/32, HQC-5 7237/7333/14421/32. Security: quasi-cyclic syndrome decoding; Xagawa found anonymity fails for two of three early parameter sets.
bitmessage_link: Different hardness assumption to lattices at 4-14 KB per ciphertext.

title: NIST SP 800-227: Recommendations for Key-Encapsulation Mechanisms
bitmessage_link: Standards-body rules for the hybrid and static-key use that a Bitmessage successor would make of ML-KEM.
note: Guidance on using KEMs: required IND-CCA properties, handling and assurance for static encapsulation keys (ownership and proof of possession), key derivation from shared secrets, and Section 4.6 on multi-algorithm KEMs and PQ/T hybrids with approved key combiners (4.6.2). Does not address recipient anonymity, so anonymity claims for ML-KEM rest on the academic proofs (Maram-Xagawa, Bao-Pan).

title: NIST IR 8547 (initial public draft): Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
note: Proposes deprecating 112-bit-strength quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2030 and disallowing all quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms (128-bit and above) after 2035; frames the harvest-now-decrypt-later risk for long-lived confidentiality.
bitmessage_link: Policy clock against which a successor's long-term confidentiality target is set.

title: Falcon: Fast-Fourier Lattice-based Compact Signatures over NTRU (specification)
venue: NIST PQC round-3 submission (basis of FN-DSA, FIPS 206 in development)
note: Sizes in bytes: Falcon-512 public key 897, signature 666 (fixed length in spec v1.2), Falcon-1024 public key 1793, signature 1280. Assumption: SIS over NTRU lattices; signing needs floating-point Gaussian sampling (side-channel and implementation hazard). Smallest post-quantum signature plus key bundle (about 1.6 KB) of the standardised families.
bitmessage_link: The least bad post-quantum signature for size-bound objects; FIPS 206 not yet final as of mid-2026.

title: CRYSTALS - Kyber: a CCA-secure module-lattice-based KEM
bitmessage_link: Origin of the primitive standardised as ML-KEM.
note: Original Kyber design (module-LWE, FO transform); round-1 sizes Kyber-768 public key 1088 B and ciphertext 1152 B before compression changes; ML-KEM-768 final is 1184/1088 B. Reference for security reductions behind ML-KEM.

title: CRYSTALS - Dilithium: A Lattice-Based Digital Signature Scheme
bitmessage_link: Origin of ML-DSA, the default replacement for per-object ECDSA.
note: Design of Dilithium (Fiat-Shamir with aborts, module-LWE/SIS); signature plus public key roughly 3.7 KB at 128-bit-class security in this early version, later growing to the FIPS 204 sizes (2420 B signature and 1312 B key for ML-DSA-44).

title: The SPHINCS+ Signature Framework
note: Stateless hash-based signature framework (basis of SLH-DSA): signatures 8-50 KB depending on parameters, public keys 32-64 B; security only from hash function properties (Grover-sensitive only quadratically).
bitmessage_link: Conservative signature option with a tiny key but unaffordable per-object size.

title: pqm4: Testing and Benchmarking NIST PQC on ARM Cortex-M4
note: Cycle-count, stack and code-size benchmarks of NIST PQC candidates on an ARM Cortex-M4 (embedded-class node), the lower bound for the cost of running post-quantum KEMs and signatures on small relays or phones.
bitmessage_link: Resource cost of the primitives on weak devices, relevant to full-node light clients.

title: Post-Quantum Authentication in TLS 1.3: A Performance Study
note: Measures how large post-quantum signatures and certificate chains inflate TLS 1.3 handshakes; lattice signatures (Dilithium, Falcon) add milliseconds, while hash-based signatures (SPHINCS+) add tens of KB and noticeably longer handshakes.
bitmessage_link: Evidence that signature size, not verification time, drives post-quantum deployment cost.

title: Benchmarking Post-Quantum Cryptography in TLS
note: Benchmarks hybrid and pure post-quantum KEM and signature combinations in TLS 1.3 under varying latency and loss; shows larger messages (multiple packets) hurt on lossy links more than computation.
bitmessage_link: Link-level cost of large post-quantum objects, relevant for gossip over weak networks.

title: Post-quantum TLS without handshake signatures
bitmessage_link: Design pattern to avoid per-session signatures: authenticate by decapsulating, as an anonymous-mailbox design could.
note: KEMTLS authenticates with KEM encapsulation to the server's long-term KEM key instead of signatures, cutting handshake bytes (a Kyber ciphertext replaces a Dilithium signature plus key) at the cost of one extra flight.

title: Transitioning to a Quantum-Resistant Public Key Infrastructure
note: Defines hybrid (dual) signatures and certificates that stay secure if either component holds, with security definitions and a performance comparison; hybrid signature size is the sum of both components (e.g. Ed25519 64 B + ML-DSA-44 2420 B).
bitmessage_link: Hybrid signature design for object authentication.

title: Benchmarking post-quantum cryptography in Ethereum-based blockchains
note: Benchmarks ECDSA against Dilithium, Falcon-1024 and SPHINCS+ on real-time Ethereum transaction data (transaction signatures only, not BLS consensus signatures). Dilithium2 verification is more than 4x faster than ECDSA (Dilithium5 2.1x) and its summed time and memory is only about 12% and 20% above ECDSA; Falcon-1024 signing takes about 224x and simplest-mode SPHINCS+ signing about 2057x ECDSA time. Signature and key sizes (Table 1) far exceed ECDSA. Author conclusion: Dilithium is the best performer; no network-load test.
bitmessage_link: Replication multiplies per-object size, as in a flooded network.

title: Technical Note: LeanSig for Post-Quantum Ethereum
note: XMSS-variant hash-based multi-signature family tuned for aggregation in Ethereum consensus gossip, trading signature size against verification hashing via an incomparable encoding; stateful hash signatures keep keys and signatures small enough for gossip when aggregated.
bitmessage_link: Design for post-quantum signatures in a gossip network where every node relays every signature.

title: Cybersecurity in an era with quantum computers: will we be ready?
note: Mosca inequality: if the time data must stay confidential (x) plus the migration time (y) exceeds the time until a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (z), the data is already at risk; gives the standard framing of record-now-decrypt-later.
bitmessage_link: Frames why a flooded, publicly stored object set (Bitmessage) is an archive for a future quantum adversary.

title: How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits
note: Resource estimate: RSA-2048 in 8 hours with 20 million noisy physical qubits (surface code, 10^-3 error). Baseline estimate for the arrival of public-key-breaking machines.
bitmessage_link: Timeline input for long-term confidentiality of recorded static-key ciphertexts.

title: How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits
note: Lowers the estimate to fewer than one million noisy physical qubits and under a week of runtime for RSA-2048 (approximate-residue arithmetic, yoked surface codes, magic-state cultivation), roughly a 20x reduction in qubits relative to 2019.
bitmessage_link: Shrinks the horizon for recorded Bitmessage ciphertexts.

title: Securing Elliptic Curve Cryptocurrencies against Quantum Vulnerabilities: Resource Estimates and Mitigations
note: Resource estimates for breaking 256-bit elliptic-curve discrete logs (the secp256k1 curve underlying Bitcoin and Bitmessage's ECDSA/ECIES keys) and mitigation paths including migration to post-quantum signatures; relevant for exposure of long-lived static public keys.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage addresses use secp256k1 keys; a quantum ECDLP solver recovers private keys from published public keys and decrypts recorded objects.

title: Implementing Grover oracles for quantum key search on AES and LowMC
note: Concrete quantum circuits for Grover against AES: key search cost for AES-128/192/256 is far above the naive sqrt(2^k) query count once circuit depth and error correction are counted, supporting treating AES-256 as comfortable and halving rather than collapsing symmetric strength.
bitmessage_link: Grover cost accounting needed to judge symmetric and hash-based parts of an object format.

title: A fast quantum mechanical algorithm for database search
note: Unstructured search in O(sqrt(N)) queries. Against an n-bit hashcash target the expected work falls from 2^n to about 2^(n/2) hash evaluations in the ideal case; it parallelises poorly (k machines give only sqrt(k) speedup).
bitmessage_link: The only generic quantum speedup for Bitmessage-style hash proof-of-work and for key search.

title: Quantum attacks on Bitcoin, and how to protect against them
note: Analyses both ECDSA breaks and Grover-based proof-of-work. For a superconducting machine (66.7 MHz gates, physical error 5e-4, difficulty 10^12) the effective hash rate is 13.8 GH/s using 4.4 million physical qubits, over 1000x slower than a 14 TH/s ASIC; scaling is about 0.04 s sqrt(D) so Grover does not parallelise like ASICs. The real exposure is ECDSA (secp256k1) key recovery from published public keys.
bitmessage_link: Directly applicable to Bitmessage's hashcash-style double-SHA-512 proof-of-work and its ECDSA keys.

title: On the insecurity of quantum Bitcoin mining
note: Argues that quantum mining speedups (including Grover) can destabilise proof-of-work consensus: a quantum miner's sub-linear scaling still leads to forks and incentives breaking down under sustained quantum advantage.
bitmessage_link: Limits of proof-of-work as an admission mechanism once quantum hardware exists.

title: The Superlinearity Problem in Post-Quantum Blockchains
note: Shows proof-of-work can be undermined by quantum computation even when all primitives are post-quantum: any puzzle with a superlinear quantum speedup (e.g. Grover) creates incentive incompatibility, and a puzzle must scale linearly in work for quantum and classical solvers to be safe. Gives constructions/impossibilities for post-quantum-sound puzzles.
bitmessage_link: Theoretical limit for using proof-of-work as spam control in a post-quantum network.

title: Lattice-Based Proof-of-Work for Post-Quantum Blockchains
note: Proof-of-work whose puzzle is a lattice problem (approximate shortest-vector/SIS-style) intended to resist quantum speedups beyond Grover while being cheap to verify; compares puzzle size and verification time with hash-based PoW.
bitmessage_link: Candidate replacement for hashcash admission control under quantum speedups.

title: Cumulative Memory Lower Bounds for Randomized and Quantum Computation
note: Proves cumulative memory complexity lower bounds for randomized and quantum circuits (extending to quantum the classical pebbling-based memory-hardness proofs); supports using memory-hard puzzles when a quantum adversary is considered, because Grover does not compress cumulative memory-time.
bitmessage_link: Theory for swapping Bitmessage's compute PoW for a memory-hard one that stays hard under quantum speedups.

title: RFC 9794: Terminology for Post-Quantum Traditional Hybrid Schemes
note: Defines vocabulary (PQ/T hybrid key encapsulation, hybrid signature, composite versus non-composite) so hybrid designs can be compared; no sizes. Reference for the hybrid KEM and hybrid signature terms used across this slice.
bitmessage_link: Common terms for the hybrid wrappers a successor would put around every key exchange.

title: RFC 10024: Post-Quantum Traditional (PQ/T) Hybrid Key Agreement Mechanisms for TLS 1.3
note: Standardises X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024. X25519MLKEM768 client share is 1216 bytes (1184 ML-KEM encapsulation key + 32 X25519) and server share 1120 bytes (1088 ML-KEM ciphertext + 32); secp256r1 variant client share carries a 65-byte point plus the 1184-byte ML-KEM key.
bitmessage_link: The deployed default hybrid; fixes the wire sizes any hybrid design is compared with.
